item.title: The Hidden Cost of Providing Too Much Comfort
item.description:
Child Development

The Hidden Cost of Providing Too Much Comfort

Distress at a new situation is not the same as an inability to handle it.

Posted August 11, 2026

Key points
  • When kids are struggling in a new situation, providing too much comfort can be an obstacle to their adapting.
  • It can send the message that we don't believe the child has what it takes to muscle through.
  • The key is to figure out the right amount of support that allows the child to work through the discomfort.

As the start of another school year draws near, I have been thinking about all the kids who may struggle with adapting to a new school or classroom, and I wanted to share a surprising insight I’ve gained as a result of the many years I’ve helped parents and teachers support kids in making this transition:

Providing too much comfort can be an obstacle to kids’ adapting, as illustrated by this story that reflects a common phenomenon.

Three weeks into the school year, I was observing in a classroom and noticed that a little guy, Ollie (4), who was new to the school, was in an assistant’s arms or on her lap for most of the day. He was singularly focused on this assistant, Marta, and not engaging at all with the other kids or adults. At circle time, he wouldn’t join the group. Marta would end up reading to him in the cozy corner. At center time, he would only play with Marta.

This was a new school for Ollie. He was understandably anxious and needed support to feel comfortable in this new environment. But by the end of the first month, there was no movement. He was still getting Marta’s 1:1 attention for much of the day and not participating in any of the group experiences. Instead of helping him discover that he could manage this new experience, the message he was internalizing was that he needed constant support and attention to adapt to being part of the group, that "someone will always help me feel better." Not, "I can handle this.”

In this case, the teachers were acting on a very common faulty mindset: that distress means inability. They were waiting for Ollie to signal to them that he was ready to engage with the group, and that if he wasn’t, it was because he couldn’t. Their constant ministering to him had inadvertently sent the message that they didn’t think he could handle it on his own.

Further, they had set an expectation that there would always be an adult to hold, carry, and engage with him 1:1—not a healthy or sustainable situation. If one adult is 1:1 with a child, it effectively means that the classroom is out of ratio. Further, a primary purpose of going to preschool is to help kids learn to feel comfortable in and thrive as part of a group.

When I suggested that a way to help Ollie work through the stress of adapting to the new class would be to reduce the support they were providing, the teaching team was uncomfortable and dubious: How could anyone who cares about and understands kids’ mental health be recommending that they withhold love and attention from a struggling child?

But once I helped them see the inadvertent message that Ollie was getting, and that there was no reason to believe he didn’t have what it takes to work this through—there were no developmental or other factors that would indicate Ollie couldn’t make a healthy transition to this new class—they were willing to give it a try.

So we developed a sensitive plan for Marta to slowly reduce her support, which required the whole team getting comfortable with Ollie’s discomfort, and not equating distress with inability. For example, when it was circle time, Marta would tell Ollie she was going to join the group and would love for him to participate when he was ready. She didn’t cajole, cheerlead, or put any pressure on him (strategies that often increase kids’ stress). When it was time for centers, she would go to the block area (she knew from Ollie’s parents that he loved to build) and collaborate with the kids in that center as they worked on their structures, hoping Ollie would eventually feel comfortable joining her and thus, his peers.

article continues after advertisement

By the third day of the “intervention,” Ollie was inching closer to the group. By day five, he was joining circle time, and on day eight, he started to participate in centers.

The Take-Home: Sometimes what feels most supportive holds kids back, and what feels mean is most loving and supportive. I see this phenomenon every day in my work with families. More comfort is not necessarily more helpful or more loving.

Another common example of this phenomenon from my practice

Josie often clings to her mom, Katie, at drop-off for taekwondo, an activity that Josie actually loves. (Note that she never has an issue when her grandma or nanny drops her off. She happily runs right in.) When Josie is acting with such desperation, it makes Katie feel like she’s harming Josie, and so she spends a lot of time comforting her—trying to get her to calm down, accept mom’s departure, and join the class. The more comfort and reassurance Katie offers, the more fiercely Josie clings and insists she won’t be OK without Katie there. Sometimes Katie throws up her hands and takes Josie home to put them both out of their misery. But she feels very uncomfortable about it, concerned that Josie is missing out on a fortifying activity, not to mention the fact that Katie doesn’t get the precious time she needs to do things for herself or run errands for the family.

After we analyze this situation together in a consult, we agree to this plan:

At drop-off, Katie will calmly share: “I know you want to stay with me right now. And I love being with you, too. But it’s time for you to learn more great taekwondo moves and for me to do my important errands. I love you and can’t wait to see you when class is over.”

Then the Master, who is aware of and has agreed to the plan, will take over as Katie leaves. He’ll show compassion: “I know, it’s hard to say bye to mommy. It’s hard for lots of kids. We are starting class today by practicing our kicks. You can join whenever you’re ready.” Then he’ll follow her lead, giving her time and space until she’s ready to participate.

Before they implement the new plan, Katie tells Josie exactly what to expect:

  • Going to the taekwondo class is a “have-to.”
  • She totally understands that separating from mom feels hard, and she has confidence Josie can manage it, just like she does when she goes to school or to play at a friend’s house.
  • At drop-off, Mom will give her a big hug and then leave. Josie’s teacher will help her move into the room and will let her know what the class will be doing that day. Then Josie can decide when she’s ready to join. That’s up to her.
  • Mom will be back when class is ending and can’t wait to hear about all the new moves she’s observed or practiced.
article continues after advertisement

The day Katie enacts the new plan, the taekwondo Master has to help Katie peel Josie off of her and guide her into the class. Katie is a wreck. But when she returns, Josie runs to her full of joy and excited to report the new skills she had learned.

In Sum

The most therapeutic thing we can communicate to a struggling child isn't: "I won't let you struggle." It's, “I know you're capable of struggling—and coming through it stronger and more confident."

item.title: On Brad Pitt’s Decision to Drink Again After 7 Years
item.description:
Addiction

On Brad Pitt’s Decision to Drink Again After 7 Years

What does it mean to be sober or in recovery?

Posted August 11, 2026

Key points
  • Brad Pitt announced that he drinks again after seven years of sobriety.
  • Some programs of recovery view abstinence as necessary, while others do not.
  • Many people commenting on Pitt’s decision are imposing their personal recovery views onto others’ journeys.

The internet is abuzz with the news that actor Brad Pitt revealed in a far-ranging interview that, “I got—I was sober for seven years. And then I got back off the wagon.” Asked about this choice, he elaborated that he drinks in a “more restrained manner. I got overconfident a couple times, went, Yep, nope, not good for me. Not in big quantities.” He further states, "I can have a few. But I can’t have a lot. I have to be professional about it.”

Pitt has been very public about his sobriety over the years. He has discussed how his divorce from Angelina Jolie prompted him to go to Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) meetings. While it was not an instant fit for him, he did find support in the AA fellowship. He publicly thanked actor Bradley Cooper at the 2020 National Board of Review Annual Awards Gala, saying, “I got sober because of this guy and every day has been happier ever since.”

Is abstinence necessary?

Why does it matter that Brad Pitt has chosen to no longer abstain from alcohol? For many in AA who believe that abstinence is the only way a person can truly be sober, Pitt’s decision seems like a mistake or a loss. His decision to drink again would be considered a relapse. As many often say of someone who has begun to drink or use again, “He’s gone back out.”

Since Pitt was so public about attending AA and acknowledging how important it was in his recovery, some worry that it will be taken as proof that AA doesn’t work. Some will always bristle when others speak publicly about their membership in AA, considering it a breach of anonymity. Because Pitt is such a public figure, his experiences are more heavily monitored and interpreted. That’s a heavy burden to put on any one individual. His experiences should not carry any more weight than anyone else’s. Nor should he be taken as a representative for AA.

Pitt’s decision also raises the question of whether abstinence is a requirement for recovery. Harm reduction approaches do not accept the premise that abstinence is necessary. Any reduction in harmful consequences of use is an improvement that may allow people to live better or even to flourish. When those negative consequences are mitigated or eliminated, a person can rightfully say that they are in recovery. Pitt’s acknowledgment of the bad consequences of his recent overindulgence fits more of a harm reduction framework.

Can you walk back a substance use disorder?

What about the American Psychiatric Association's definition of substance use disorder (SUD)? The diagnosis comprises 11 criteria that are met over the course of 12 months. A person who meets two to three criteria has a mild SUD, meeting four to five criteria is a moderate SUD, while meeting six or more criteria is a severe SUD. That leaves open the possibility that someone who met two or more of the criteria but no longer does may be able to consume their drug of choice and no longer have a SUD. If there is no SUD, there is no relapse. Perhaps this is how Pitt views the regression of drinking and using patterns. He had a problem, and he walked it back.

We humans are always changing; those of us in recovery (however each of us defines it) can point to so many ways that we have changed for the better. What we need in recovery may change as well. Someone who has tried to moderate their use may decide to become abstinent. Others may turn to medication-assisted therapies instead of trying to quit “cold turkey.” Others may decide that abstinence is not a good or right choice for them now.

What does Pitt’s drinking mean for other people in recovery?

No doubt many people with the best of intentions do not want to see Pitt suffer the terrible consequences that often follow from an addiction. It is possible that those consequences will follow after drinking again. It is also possible they will not follow.

Other people who are less charitable may be waiting to see him fail or return to his worst using days. They may mistakenly take this as proof that their approach to sobriety and recovery is the only good/true/right one. That’s an unjustified conclusion.

I have written elsewhere about "sobersplainers." People who sobersplain tend to act as authorities on what others need to do to be in recovery. They are not just experts on their own recovery, but they act as experts on everyone else’s recovery. There is a lot of sobersplaining happening right now from what I am seeing on various social media.

This is Brad Pitt’s decision to make and live with. It is not my place to judge him but only to wish him well.

item.title: The New Wire(d) Mother
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

The New Wire(d) Mother

How artificial intelligence reshapes our experience of human relationships.

Posted August 11, 2026

Key points
  • Many individuals are using artificial intelligence to replace needs historically met in relationships.
  • AI can mimic empathy, but it cannot offer real empathy.
  • Relying on AI for connection deepens isolation and erodes vital human relational skills.

Artificial intelligence (AI) has evolved rapidly over the last several years, with people growing increasingly attached to it. The various versions of AI have been described as having different personalities or personality traits (Jędrzejczak & Kobosko, 2025), with individuals developing strong attachments to certain versions. Many became particularly attached to GPT-4o, for example, with people reporting grieving and even having funerals when this version went away (Demopoulos, 2026).

Recent years have witnessed a rise in technology use that has even been described as similar to addiction. Mental health professionals have voiced concern that technology is replacing human-to-human relationships, contributing to increased isolation and loneliness, combined with deteriorating interpersonal skills (Hoffman & Hoffman, 2026; Schneider, 2019). Now, as individuals increasingly rely upon AI to write or polish emails, text messages, and letters, technology is being further inserted between human interactions. Given the accelerating pace of AI advancement and use, research and exploration of the ethics of AI are lagging.

At the 2026 American Psychological Association Annual Convention in August, AI companies were featured prominently as sponsors, and a wealth of presentations focused on AI. Diverse responses include mental health professionals scrambling to issue warnings, rapidly integrating AI into their practice, and finding opportunities in AI development. While some therapists worry about being replaced, others maintain confidence that AI will remain unable to replace the human elements of psychotherapy and recognize ways AI may contribute to a growing need for the depth and relational aspects of therapy (Hoffman, 2024).

Source: Louis Hoffman, PhD

Harlow’s Monkeys

In the 1950s, Harry Harlow (1958; Harlow & Zimmermann, 1959) conducted his famous studies in which infant rhesus monkeys were separated from their mothers but offered two alternatives: a wire mother alternative that provided milk and a cloth mother alternative that in some studies provided milk and in others did not. Regardless of whether the cloth surrogate mother offered milk, it was preferred over the wire mother. When only the wire surrogate was present with no cloth mother, the infant monkeys still stayed in proximity to the wire version, but there was less emotional security evident in their behavior. Across the studies, the infant monkeys fared worse when there was no cloth surrogate option and when they were more isolated.

As AI and other forms of technology increasingly replace aspects of relationships that historically were met by primary attachment figures and close relationships, such as family and friends, the question can be asked as to whether the lessons from Harlow’s experiments may have renewed relevance. Harlow’s monkeys suffered when their social needs were met by technological means, such as the artificial bottles and constructed replications of attachment figures. While the monkeys survived, even grew comparatively in size and weight, they did not emotionally or socially flourish.

The Impact of AI on the Experience of Relationships

In Ovsyannikova et al.’s (2025) study on empathy, participants often rated empathetic statements constructed by AI as more compassionate than those constructed by people. However, when they found out that these statements were constructed by AI, their experience of them changed to being less positive. A much larger study by Rubin et al. (2025) adds important nuance. While their study also found positive appraisals of AI responses that mimicked empathy, their results indicated that individuals chose to discuss certain topics with AI rather than with a human due to what they were seeking and the nature of the concerns. For example, participants tended to choose AI when curious about how AI might respond or when they were worried about how a human might respond, such as concerns about feeling judged. Additionally, when participants perceived the response as being from AI or aided by AI, the positive effects were reduced. Importantly, responses perceived to be by a human were less likely to contribute to negative emotions.

Empathetic statements are not the same as empathy (Bohart et al., 2025; Hoffman, 2020; Rubin et al., 2025). Increasingly, empathy has been reduced in the mental health field to a technique instead of an embodied experience. Yet, acting empathetic is not the same as being empathetic, and when empathy is a performance or technique instead of embodied, it often leads to feelings of hurt, anger, alienation, and objectification (Hoffman, 2020; see also Hoffman & Hoffman, 2026). While AI can mimic empathy, it cannot offer empathy. The deeper healing qualities of empathy are those that are embodied: the shared feelings, the openness to being moved by someone else, and care, concern, and love for the other person. When people experience wired empathy (i.e., the simulation of empathy by AI), it does not impact people in the same way as embodied empathy.

An important part of what bonds and sustains us in relationships is vulnerability and personal sharing. Vulnerability, however, is not easy, particularly on topics that the person experiences as shameful. While it may be easier to disclose personal thoughts, behaviors, and feelings that are shameful with an AI platform or bot, this serves to disconnect us from deeper forms of support and community in human relationships. New forms of isolation and loneliness emerge as people turn to technology for needs better filled by other people.

Conclusion

When AI replaces important aspects of human social relationships and community, it contributes to a deepening of isolation. AI is not going away, and the ways that it is used will undoubtedly expand. As we move deeper into this age of AI, it is critical that we consider its potential impacts on essential aspects of being human and strive to preserve these precious parts of our existence.

item.title: Autism and Vaccines: Questions Science Hasn’t Settled
item.description:
Autism

Autism and Vaccines: Questions Science Hasn’t Settled

Polarization obscures the need for nuanced, systems-level research on vaccines.

Posted August 11, 2026

The vaccine-autism debate has become so polarized that two different scientific questions are often treated as though they were the same.

The first is:

Is vaccination, across populations, associated with a large increase in autism? Large epidemiological studies have generally not demonstrated such an association.

The second is more biologically specific:

Could vaccination sometimes become one component of a larger cumulative inflammatory or physiological threat load that, in a susceptible developing child, contributes to altered neurodevelopment? That question has not been definitively answered.

A Common Biological Pathway: Proinflammatory Threat Signaling

Threat-based proinflammatory cytokines—including IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, IL-8, and related mediators—are not merely markers of inflammation. They participate in coordinated whole-system responses to infection, injury, and other threats.

When sufficiently elevated or persistent, this signaling can produce a recognizable physiological phenotype involving cardiovascular instability, respiratory dysregulation, metabolic alteration and catabolism, autonomic disruption, altered cortical excitability, seizures, encephalopathy, impaired consciousness, and, at extreme intensity, circulatory shock.

The response depends upon concentration, duration, developmental stage, underlying physiology, and the surrounding signaling environment. Cytokines interact with prostaglandins, nitric oxide, purines ATP and adenosine, endothelial pathways, cortisol, catecholamines, and neural circuits. The relevant biological phenomenon is therefore not a single cytokine but an integrated threat-response network.

In premature infants, vaccination has been shown to produce measurable inflammatory activation. Pourcyrous and colleagues demonstrated elevations in C-reactive protein (CRP) following immunization, with apnea, bradycardia, and oxygen desaturation occurring in some infants. Underlying vulnerability and multiple injections were associated with greater cardiorespiratory instability.

This does not demonstrate autism or permanent neurological injury following vaccination. It establishes a narrower but important point: Vaccination can contribute measurably to systemic cytokine-governed physiology, and the magnitude and clinical expression of that response can vary with the condition of the host.

Threats and the Developing Brain

Independent of vaccination, pediatric and neonatal research demonstrates associations between significant early threat cytokine activation and neurological function.

Elevated threat and inflammatory signaling have been associated with altered cortical excitability, febrile seizures, neonatal encephalopathy, cardiorespiratory instability, and adverse developmental outcomes.

The ELGAN (extremely low gestational age newborns) studies are particularly important because investigators measured inflammatory proteins rather than merely inferring inflammation from an exposure. Persistent elevations of inflammatory mediators in extremely premature infants have been associated with later cerebral palsy, cognitive impairment, and other neurodevelopmental abnormalities.

More recent follow-up has linked neonatal inflammatory profiles with measurable differences in adolescent brain structure. Sustained elevations of inflammatory proteins, including IL-6, TNF-α, IL-8, CRP, serum amyloid A, and ICAM-1, were associated with smaller volumes in several brain regions at age 15.

These observations establish an important principle: The intensity and persistence of threat-associated physiology during vulnerable periods of development can be associated with subsequent nervous-system structure and function.

They do not establish what caused every threat-associated episode, and they do not establish vaccination as the cause of autism.

Vaccines Are One Potential Input Into a Larger System

Vaccines are designed to stimulate immune recognition, so some inflammatory signaling is expected. For most children, this response is transient and resolves without lasting consequence. Vaccination also prevents infections capable of producing far greater threat response, inflammation, and neurological injury.

But population-level safety does not logically establish that the physiological contribution of vaccination must equal zero in every individual under every circumstance.

Vaccination should therefore be considered neither the presumed cause nor an automatically excluded variable. It is one potential input into a much larger biological system.

At the moment of vaccination, a child's total threat load might also include infection, prematurity, sleep disruption, nutritional or metabolic abnormalities, pollutants, medications, gastrointestinal inflammation, prenatal or maternal inflammation, genetic susceptibility, epigenetic programming, psychosocial stress, socioeconomic adversity, and previous immune activation.

The important question may therefore not be: How many vaccine antigens did the child receive?

It may instead be: What was the child's physiological state before exposure, what physiologic response followed, how intense and persistent was it, did it resolve normally, and what happened to brain function during and after that response?

Those variables have not been comprehensively measured in the major vaccine-autism epidemiological studies.

What the 2013 Antigen Study Actually Tested

The frequently cited DeStefano et al. 2013 study did not create a new prospective cohort designed specifically to examine simultaneous vaccination.

It performed a secondary analysis of the case-control population previously used in the Price et al. 2010 thimerosal study—256 children with ASD and 752 controls—and reconstructed antigen exposure from vaccination records.

It provides useful evidence against a simple hypothesis that increasing numbers of vaccine antigens produce a corresponding increase in population-level autism risk.

But antigen count is not inflammatory physiology.

The study did not serially measure cytokines, chemokines, CRP, purinergic signaling, cortisol, catecholamines, metabolic responses, autonomic function, or cortical activity surrounding vaccination. Nor was it designed to determine whether a small susceptible subgroup experienced an unusual physiological response.

It therefore answers an important question, but not every plausible mechanistic question.

The Study That Still Needs to Be Done

The definitive test would require a large prospective longitudinal birth cohort examining the child as an integrated biological system.

Before vaccination, investigators would characterize genetics, relevant epigenetics, gestational and birth history, developmental status, infections, medications, nutrition, sleep, metabolic state, environmental exposures, psychosocial stress, and other contributors to a threat load and the associated systemic response.

Exact vaccines, combinations, timing, and spacing would be recorded.

Immediately before and repeatedly after vaccination, investigators would measure markers and mediators such as IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, IL-8, interferons, chemokines, and CRP; ATP/adenosine and other purinergic markers; cortisol and catecholamines; metabolic parameters; endothelial and oxidative-stress markers; and immune-cell phenotypes.

Physiological monitoring would include heart rate, heart rate variability, respiration and apnea, oxygen saturation, blood pressure, temperature, sleep, and activity.

Most importantly, brain function should be measured rather than inferred.

Age-appropriate EEG could assess cortical excitability, connectivity, and network activity. Where feasible, longitudinal structural MRI, diffusion imaging, resting-state functional MRI, and spectroscopy could examine cortical, thalamocortical, cerebellar, brainstem, and large-scale network development.

Particular attention should be directed toward the higher-order cortical and network functions altered in autism, including distinctly human networks involved in sensory integration, attention, emotional-social integration, executive function, and language.

Children would then be followed longitudinally with repeated assessments of sensory integration, attention, emotional-social integration, executive function, language acquisition, adaptive behavior, and autism-related developmental measures.

The critical analysis would test interactions:

baseline susceptibility × existing threat load × vaccine exposure × immune-inflammatory and metabolic-endocrine response × cortical response × resolution time × developmental trajectory.

That is the systems-level experiment capable of testing the hypothesis.

Beyond the Polarization

Existing epidemiology provides substantial reassurance that routine vaccination is not associated with a large population-wide increase in autism and defines substantial benefit to vaccinations.

At the same time, developmental biology demonstrates that substantial or persistent threat-associated activation can alter cardiovascular, respiratory, metabolic, and neurological function and can correlate with subsequent differences in brain development.

Vaccination can generate threat signaling and therefore belongs among the biological exposures considered when studying total immunologic-inflammatory or threat load. That does not establish vaccination as a cause of autism. It means vaccination should neither automatically be assigned causality nor removed from a comprehensive causal model before the relevant physiology has actually been measured.

The scientifically defensible conclusion is therefore neither “vaccines cause autism” nor “every conceivable contribution of vaccination to autism has already been disproved.”

We have strong population-level evidence against a simple vaccine-autism relationship. What we do not yet have is the comprehensive prospective mechanistic study capable of determining whether unusual systemic responses to vaccination—or to any other exposure—interacting with existing biological and environmental threat loads in susceptible children can contribute to developmental change.

Polarization becomes scientifically counterproductive when one side treats temporal association as proof of causation while the other treats reassuring population epidemiology as a reason to stop investigating mechanism, susceptibility, and biological heterogeneity.

The answer is not greater certainty than the evidence permits.

Fund and perform the definitive study—and replace polarization with data.

item.title: Needing Others Doesn’t Make You Needy
item.description:
Relationships

Needing Others Doesn’t Make You Needy

Seeking healthy connection helps us grow without losing ourselves.

Posted August 11, 2026

Key points
  • Needing other people is a basic psychological need, not a sign of weakness.
  • Autonomy and relatedness can coexist; connection does not require losing yourself.
  • The goal should not be to need less, but to depend on others without surrendering your sense of self.

Think about the last time something wonderful happened to you. Maybe you received a promotion, finished a difficult project, heard good news about your health, or watched your child accomplish something meaningful. What did you do next? When this happens to me, I know what I want to do. I want to tell someone. I want to share my joy. But posting about it online doesn’t give me what I need.

If you are like me, that impulse reveals something important about us. Success is not only something we want to experience privately or performatively. It becomes fuller when it is shared, celebrated with friends and family, and folded into relationships. The same is true for hardships. We may be embarrassed or ashamed to go through something hard, and we may be hesitant to “publicize” our pain, but when we receive a sympathetic ear or a helping hand, we appreciate more than just the assistance. We are grateful for being seen and for the interpersonal connection.

We often talk as though needing other people is a sign of weakness. “Don’t be so needy.” “Learn to be independent.” “You have to be enough for yourself.” These phrases contain good advice in context, especially when they warn us against becoming so dependent on others that we lose a healthy sense of self. Yet, when turned into blanket advice, these “warnings” can also hide an important truth: emotionally healthy people need others in their lives.

Simon and Garfunkel might sing, “I am a rock. I am an island,” but if we believe this for ourselves, that is not strength; it’s denial.

Human beings do not merely need others to provide food, shelter, information, or assistance. We need their presence and connection. A 2023 study of 48,550 people across 27 European countries found that satisfying one’s need for relatedness, defined as the innate human need to feel connected, cared for, and a sense of belonging with others, was associated with greater happiness, life satisfaction, meaning, and fewer depressive symptoms in every country studied.

These findings fit within the broader psychological framework of self-determination theory, which holds that people are naturally motivated to grow and flourish when three basic psychological needs are met: autonomy, competence, and relatedness. Self-determination theory dovetails with Roy Baumeister and Mark Leary’s influential argument that the need to belong, to form and maintain stable, caring relationships, is a fundamental human motivation. We do not begin life as fully independent individuals who later decide whether relationships might enhance our well-being. Our relationships help shape who we become as we develop.

Needing others versus being needy

While the need to relate to others is a psychological need, “neediness” is not a clinical category. However, psychologists have studied behaviors that can resemble what we commonly mean by the colloquial term. For example, excessive reassurance-seeking is the relatively stable tendency to seek assurances excessively and persistently from others that one is lovable and worthy, regardless of whether it has already been provided. The problem, then, is not occasionally wanting reassurance from someone with whom we have a relationship. It arises when we repeatedly need another person to establish that we are lovable or that the relationship is secure.

To explain the distinction: Relatedness is the need to share one’s life with others; excessive reassurance-seeking stems from the need to confirm our worth through others.

Connection need not come at the expense of independence

Relatedness is not the same as losing yourself in another person, just as autonomy does not require complete independence or detachment from others. Nor are autonomy and relatedness competing psychological needs. Kluwer, Karremans, Riedijk, and Knee have shown that people report more constructive relationship-maintenance behavior when their needs for relatedness and autonomy are both satisfied. In this context, autonomy does not mean separateness; it means retaining a sense of agency and self-direction while remaining connected to others. Moreover, through what psychologist Brooke Feeney calls the dependency paradox, when close partners respond sensitively to legitimate needs for support, that support can foster greater autonomy and self-sufficiency rather than greater dependence.

Sometimes knowing that someone is there for us is precisely what enables us to stand on our own.

Seeking out healthy dependence

A healthy need for connection and relationship allows us to remain ourselves while allowing other people to remain themselves. We can want closeness without demanding or giving up complete control. We can seek guidance without requiring someone else to organize their entire life around our insecurity. We can depend on people while still maintaining a sense of self.

We can need others without being needy.

The challenge is not to need less, but to need wisely; to seek relationships where people can share their joy, speak in their own voices, grow into themselves, and still know that they do not have to face life alone.
